group.title: Crime and safety
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A person who takes things that belong to someone else.
examples: The {thief} ran off with my bag.
wrong: The thief kindly gave back everything and never took anything.

words.meaning: The crime of taking something that is not yours.
examples: She reported the {theft} of her bike to the police.
wrong: The theft happened when he paid for the bike at the shop.

words.meaning: A person who goes into a building to take things.
examples: A {burglar} climbed in through the kitchen window.
wrong: The burglar was a guest we invited for dinner.

words.meaning: The crime of entering a home or building to take things.
examples: There was a {burglary} on our street last night.
wrong: The burglary was a friendly visit from our neighbor.

words.meaning: The crime of taking money or things from a person or place, often with force.
examples: Two men were arrested after the bank {robbery}.
wrong: The robbery was a gift the bank gave its customers.

words.meaning: To take money or things from a person or place illegally.
examples: Someone {robbed} the shop and took all the cash.
wrong: He robbed the shop by paying for everything he bought.

words.meaning: To take something that is not yours without asking.
examples: Somebody {stole} my phone on the train.
wrong: She stole the cake by buying it at the bakery.

words.meaning: When the police take someone away because they may have done a crime.
examples: The police {arrested} the driver for speeding.
wrong: The police arrested him to thank him for his help.

words.meaning: A police officer or private agent whose job is to find out who did a crime.
examples: The {detective} looked for clues in the room.
wrong: The detective’s job is to hide the facts about a crime.

words.meaning: Having done a crime or something wrong.
examples: The court found him {guilty} of theft.
wrong: He was guilty, so he had done nothing wrong at all.

words.meaning: Not having done a crime or anything wrong.
examples: She was {innocent}; someone else took the money.
wrong: He was innocent because he had stolen the car.

words.meaning: The place where a judge decides if someone broke the law.
examples: The case will go to {court} next month.
wrong: The court is where people go to buy fresh vegetables.

words.meaning: The person in charge of a trial who decides on the punishment.
examples: The {judge} sent him to prison for two years.
wrong: The judge was the man who stole the car.

words.meaning: A building where people who have done crimes are kept.
examples: He spent three months in {jail}.
wrong: After the crime he went to jail for a holiday by the sea.

words.meaning: To make someone suffer because they did something wrong.
examples: The school {punished} the boys for breaking the window.
wrong: They punished her with a prize for her good work.

words.meaning: Not allowed by the law.
examples: It is {illegal} to drive without a license.
wrong: Walking in the park is illegal, so everyone does it.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to give advice about the law and speak for people in court.
examples: Her {lawyer} spoke to the judge for her.
wrong: The lawyer fixed my car engine in court.

words.meaning: A device that makes a loud noise to warn people of danger.
examples: The {alarm} went off when the burglar opened the door.
wrong: The alarm stayed silent, so it warned everyone loudly.

words.meaning: The state of being protected from danger or harm.
examples: Wear a helmet for your {safety}.
wrong: For his safety, he drove fast without a seat belt.

words.meaning: Something used to hurt or kill people, such as a gun.
examples: The police found a {weapon} in his car.
wrong: He used a pillow as a weapon to fall asleep.

words.meaning: The crime of killing a person on purpose.
examples: The detective solved the {murder} in a week.
wrong: The murder was a nice party for his friend.

words.meaning: A person who has broken the law.
examples: The {criminal} was caught on camera.
wrong: The criminal had always obeyed every law.

words.meaning: A person paid to protect a building and the people in it.
examples: The {security guard} checked our bags at the door.
wrong: The security guard was paid to steal from the shop.

words.meaning: To tell someone about a danger or problem before it happens.
examples: The sign {warns} drivers about the ice.
wrong: He warned me about the storm after it had passed.

words.meaning: The crime of taking things from a store without paying.
examples: The girl was caught {shoplifting} sweets.
wrong: Shoplifting is when you pay for your food at the till.

words.meaning: A thief who quietly takes wallets and phones from people in crowds.
examples: A {pickpocket} took my wallet on the crowded bus.
wrong: The pickpocket put money into my pocket as a present.

words.meaning: The crime of damaging public or private property on purpose.
examples: The broken bus stop was an act of {vandalism}.
wrong: The vandalism made the park cleaner and more beautiful.

words.meaning: The mark left on a surface by the tiny lines on the tip of your thumb or other digits.
examples: The police found his {fingerprints} on the glass.
wrong: She left a fingerprint on the window with her shoe.

words.meaning: To get away from a place where you are kept.
examples: Two prisoners {escaped} from the jail.
wrong: He escaped from prison by staying in his cell.

words.meaning: To save someone from a dangerous situation.
examples: Firefighters {rescued} the family from the fire.
wrong: They rescued the swimmer by leaving him in the sea.

words.meaning: To say you will hurt someone if they do not do what you want.
examples: The man {threatened} to hit him.
wrong: She threatened him by giving him a warm hug.

words.meaning: To hurt or frighten someone smaller or weaker again and again.
examples: The older boys {bullied} him at school.
wrong: She bullied her friend by helping her with homework.

words.meaning: A dishonest plan to get money from people.
examples: The email about free money was a {scam}.
wrong: The scam was an honest offer that helped everyone.

words.meaning: To enter a building or car by force to take things.
examples: Someone {broke into} my car last night.
wrong: He broke into his house with his own key.

words.meaning: Making you think something is wrong or illegal.
examples: Call the police if you see a {suspicious} bag.
wrong: The bag looked suspicious, so it looked completely normal.

words.meaning: A group of police or guards that moves around an area to keep it safe.
examples: A police {patrol} drives through the area every night.
wrong: The patrol stays at home and never visits the streets.

words.meaning: To say that someone has done something wrong.
examples: They {accused} him of stealing the money.
wrong: She accused him of being honest and kind.

words.meaning: To admit that you did something wrong or illegal.
examples: He finally {confessed} to the robbery.
wrong: He confessed by saying he had done nothing wrong.

words.meaning: A device that films a place so that crimes can be seen and recorded.
examples: The {security camera} filmed the thief.
wrong: The security camera is used to cook dinner.

words.meaning: Not allowed by the rules of a country.
examples: Stealing is {against the law}.
wrong: Helping old people cross the road is against the law.
